blocks.md: You have a list of products. You want prices only. You want only the in-stock ones. You want to run a side effect for each. This is the daily bread of JavaScript — and four array methods do almost all of it: `forEach`, `map`, `filter`, and `find`. Master these and you stop writing manual `for` loops forever.

blocks.canDo: transform data with map, filter, forEach and find
blocks.md: By the end of this session you will be able to use `forEach` to iterate, `map` to transform every item into something new, `filter` to keep only matching items, and `find` to locate the first match — and know which one to reach for in any situation.

**The four workhorses**

- **`forEach(fn)`** — calls `fn` for every item; returns `undefined`. Use it for side effects (logging, DOM updates). It does *not* build a new array.
- **`map(fn)`** — calls `fn` for every item and *collects the return values* into a new array of the same length. Use it to transform: prices → discounted prices, objects → JSX elements.
- **`filter(fn)`** — calls `fn` for every item and keeps only items where `fn` returns truthy. The result array is the same length *or shorter*.
- **`find(fn)`** — returns the *first* item where `fn` returns truthy, or `undefined` if nothing matches. Stops as soon as it finds one.

All four receive the same callback signature: `(item, index, array)` — though you rarely need all three arguments. None of them mutate the original array.
Read this freeCodeCamp article — it walks through `map`, `filter`, and `reduce` with clear before/after examples. Focus on the `map` and `filter` sections; skim `reduce` for now.

blocks.md:
**Pick the right tool**

| Goal | Method |
|---|---|
| Run a side effect for each item | `forEach` |
| Build a new array of the same length | `map` |
| Build a shorter array of matching items | `filter` |
| Get one matching item | `find` |

If you find yourself calling `map` but ignoring the return value, switch to `forEach`. If you find yourself filtering and then mapping, you can chain: `arr.filter(…).map(…)`.

questions.question: What does `[1, 2, 3].map(x => x * 2)` return?
questions.explanation: `map` returns a new array of the same length where each item is the result of the callback — so each number is doubled.

questions.question: You call `[10, 20, 30].filter(n => n > 15)`. What do you get?
questions.explanation: `filter` keeps only items for which the callback returns truthy. 20 and 30 are both greater than 15, so they are kept; 10 is dropped.

questions.question: Which method should you use when you want to log every item in an array but do NOT need a new array back?
questions.explanation: `forEach` is designed for side effects. It always returns `undefined`, so it signals clearly that you are not building a new array.

blocks.md: You now have the four array methods that cover the vast majority of real-world data work in JavaScript.
bullets: `forEach` — iterate for side effects, returns nothing
`map` — transform every item, returns a new array of the same length
`filter` — keep matching items, returns a shorter (or equal-length) array
`find` — locate the first match, returns one item or `undefined`
